newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan leads in inconclusive U.N. race.
newsitem.headline: Annan leads in inconclusive U.N. race.

text.p: Two rounds of unofficial balloting for the post of U.N. secretary-general ended inconclusively on Tuesday, with all four African candidates getting at least one potential veto from a permanent member of the Security Council.

Kofi Annan of Ghana, the U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping, led in the more important second round of informal voting and was the only candidate to get more than the nine votes required, diplomats said.
But he received one negative vote from a permanent member, said to be France, which prefers candidates from its former French-speaking colonies.

The 15-member council held two rounds of unofficial polls, with its five permanent veto-bearing members -- the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France -- voting with marked ballots in the second round only.
Diplomats said the following count emerged on a second ballot of voting:
-- Kofi Annan -- 10 votes in favour, four against, one of them from a permanent member.
-- Amara Essy, the Ivory Coast's foreign minister -- seven votes in favour, four against, two of them from permanent members.
-- Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference -- five votes in favour, seven against, two of them permanent members.

-- Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania, a former U.N. special envoy for Burundi who now heads the Washington-based Global Coalition for Africa -- three votes in favour, seven against, two of them from permanent members.
Diplomats suspected that the United States and Britain cast negative votes against all candidates except Annan.

It is not known how many straw polls the council will take or when official voting will begin for the race, which is still deadlocked. The next round of balloting will be on Wednesday said Council President Paolo Fulci of Italy.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali was vetoed by the United States in a Nov. 19 vote in which all the other 14 council members supported him for a second term.

He suspended his candidacy on Dec. 4. He could reactivate it at any time but if he does he is all but certain to encounter another veto by the United States, which insists the United Nations needs new leadership to implement reforms.

All the candidates so far are from Africa. The council is giving that continent priority on the grounds that if the U.S. veto denies the Egyptian incumbent the second term enjoyed by his predecessors, his successor should be another African.
Fulci would not give any details of the voting after the closed-door council meeting ended.
"In Rome, when the cardinals are locked up in the Sistine Chapel to elect the Pope they are forbidden to say anything outside," he said.
"If a new Pope has not been elected, black smoke comes out of the chimney," he added. "The moment the Pope is elected, white smoke comes out of the chimney."
"The smoke coming out of the room tonight is black," he said. "We will try again at 11:30 a.m. (1630 GMT) tomorrow morning."
